sections.h2: How does a Georgia tax sale work?
sections.html:
A Georgia tax sale is a public auction of a delinquent property after a tax lien has been issued and the property has been advertised. The winning bidder receives a tax deed, and the owner keeps a right to buy the property back. Sales run under O.C.G.A. 48-3-1 and 48-4-1 and following, as the DeKalb County conditions of sale state.

The county sets the calendar. DeKalb holds sales on the first Tuesday of the month from April through December on the courthouse steps in Decatur. Cobb holds them on the first Tuesday of the months it plans a sale, moving to Wednesday if Tuesday is a holiday. Gwinnett says it generally holds sales in only a few selected months.

Opening bids are the unpaid taxes plus penalties, interest, and costs. Georgia sells the deed, and the lien itself is not what changes hands, a point Cobb stresses by stating that it sells tax deeds and does not sell tax liens.

sections.h2: What does a bidder have to do on sale day?
sections.html:
Registration comes first. Cobb requires pre-registration for each sale and issues bidder cards between 9:00 and 10:00 a.m. on the day, against a photo ID. DeKalb requires registration for each sale as well, either online beforehand or in person that morning.

  • Payment. Cobb wants payment in full when the sale ends, by cash or certified check. DeKalb's conditions require cash, a cashier's check or a certified check from an insured institution within one hour after the sale ends.
  • Failure to pay. DeKalb says an unpaid bid goes back up for resale the same afternoon, and the defaulting bidder may owe the difference or be barred from later sales.
  • Unsold parcels. Cobb may re-auction properties that drew no bid at 3 p.m. that afternoon.
  • Buyer beware. DeKalb's conditions state that the doctrine of caveat emptor applies to every tax sale.

For an owner, the same details matter in reverse: once a sale is scheduled, DeKalb accepts only cash, bank cashier's checks or bank wires, and Gwinnett accepts only certified funds.

sections.h2: How long can the owner take the property back?
sections.html:
At least 12 months, and often longer. O.C.G.A. 48-4-40 lets the defendant in the execution, or anyone with a right, title, interest or lien in the property, redeem within 12 months of the sale, and after that until the right is cut off by the statutory notice.

Georgia's redemption price is set by 48-4-42. The table below lists the pieces as the Department of Revenue course text prints them for sales after July 1, 2002.

What the redemption payment includes under O.C.G.A. 48-4-42
ComponentRule as printed
BidThe amount paid at the tax sale, as shown in the tax deed
Later taxesAny taxes the purchaser paid after the sale
Special assessmentsAny special assessments on the property
Premium20 percent for the first year or fraction of a year since the sale, then 10 percent for each additional year or fraction of a year
Notice costsSheriff's cost for serving the notice and publication costs, if redemption comes more than 30 days after the foreclosure notice
Association sumsFor sales after July 1, 2016, certain amounts paid to a property owners', condominium or homeowners' association

Payment goes to the purchaser in lawful United States money. Cobb adds that the tax sale purchaser is responsible for working out the redemption amount, so ask the purchaser or the tax commissioner for a written figure.

sections.h2: Can the purchaser move in right after the sale?
sections.html:
No. Cobb's tax commissioner states that the purchaser gets a tax deed but cannot take possession, make improvements, evict tenants or move onto the property. Gwinnett says buyers at a sale do not automatically own the property and owners are not immediately evicted.

The purchaser can end the owner's right to redeem only by following the notice rules in 48-4-45. After 12 months the purchaser serves notice on the defendant in the execution, the occupant, and everyone with a recorded interest or lien in the county, and must publish it once a week for four consecutive weeks in the sheriff's advertisement newspaper. Notice to people outside the county goes by registered or certified mail or statutory overnight delivery.

Even then the deed is not final overnight. Under 48-4-48 a tax deed executed at a valid sale after July 1, 1996 ripens into fee simple title four years after the deed is recorded in the county land records.

sections.h2: What if I redeem the property or the sale brings in extra money?
sections.html:
Redemption puts the title back in the owner, subject to every lien that existed at the time of the sale, according to 48-4-43. The purchaser must then sign a quitclaim deed to the owner under 48-4-44, naming who paid the redemption money. If it is not presented at redemption, the purchaser has seven days to supply one properly witnessed, and it must reach the clerk of the superior court within ten days of the redemption. Our quitclaim deed guide explains that kind of deed.

When a sale brings in more than taxes and costs, the extra money belongs to the parties with an interest. Cobb says its tax commissioner may file an interpleader in superior court to distribute it, and DeKalb holds excess funds until a rightful party files a claim. DeKalb accepts claims only from the entitled party or a Georgia attorney, and not from an agent under a power of attorney.

sections.h2: How does the court-supervised sale differ?
sections.html:
Counties and cities that adopt the process under 48-4-76 can foreclose through superior court instead. The sale is advertised as sheriffs' sales are, cannot occur earlier than 45 days after the court's order, and the minimum bid is the redemption amount.

The owner's redemption window is shorter, 60 days after the sale, and the owner redeems by paying the minimum bid price into the superior court. Within 90 days after the sale, the petitioner must deliver the deed and file a report of the sale. Any surplus above the minimum bid is deposited with the court and distributed by priority to the interested parties, including the owner.

sections.h2: Can I sell my Georgia house before a tax sale?
sections.html:
Yes, a sale to a buyer that closes before the auction can pay the delinquent taxes out of the proceeds. The county will treat payment of everything owed as a stop to the sale, and Gwinnett confirms that the owner can pay all taxes, costs and fees after a property is selected for sale, in certified funds. Ask the tax commissioner for a payoff figure through your closing date, since advertising and title research fees keep being added as the sale approaches.

If the auction has already taken place, the 12 month redemption period is the next deadline. A buyer purchasing from you then has to account for the purchaser's rights as well, so involve a Georgia real estate attorney and a title company early.

faqs.q: Where are Georgia tax sales held?
faqs.a: At the county, usually at the courthouse. DeKalb holds them on the courthouse steps in Decatur, Cobb at the Superior Court Plaza, and Gwinnett in front of the Justice and Administration Center in Lawrenceville.

faqs.q: How long do I have to redeem after a Georgia tax sale?
faqs.a: At least 12 months from the sale date. After that the right continues until the purchaser cuts it off by giving the statutory foreclosure notice to the owner, the occupant and recorded interest holders.

The purchaser's bid, plus later taxes the purchaser paid, special assessments, and a premium of 20 percent for the first year or fraction and 10 percent for each additional year or fraction. Notice costs may be added. Get the exact figure in writing.

faqs.q: Does the buyer at a tax sale own the house immediately?
faqs.a: No. The buyer holds a tax deed that works like a lien until redemption rights end. Cobb says the purchaser cannot take possession, improve the property or evict tenants during that time.

faqs.q: What happens to extra money from a tax sale?
faqs.a: It is held for the parties entitled to it. DeKalb takes claims from the entitled party or a Georgia attorney, and Cobb may file an interpleader action in superior court to distribute the money.
